title: Effects of Remote Ischemic Conditioning on Cerebral Blood Flow Regulation in Atherosclerosis: A Randomized Trial
content:
In this randomized controlled trial, a single session of remote ischemic conditioning (RIC) was evaluated in patients with intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ICAS) and/or extracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ECAS). Dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) was assessed at baseline and at 0–1, 6–9, and 24 h. At the prespecified 6–9 h primary outcome, RIC significantly increased affected-side phase difference compared with sham-RIC, supporting a rapid improvement in dCA.


ABSTRACT

Impaired dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) contributes to cerebral perfusion instability in patients with cerebrovascular atherosclerosis. Remote ischemic conditioning (RIC) has shown neuroprotective potential; however, its acute effects on dCA in this population remain unclear. In this randomized, sham-controlled trial, patients with intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ICAS) and/or extracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ECAS) received a single session of RIC or sham-RIC. dCA was assessed at baseline and at 0–1, 6–9, and 24 h using transfer function analysis. The prespecified primary endpoint was the affected-side phase difference (PD) at 6–9 h. Of the 140 randomized participants, 132 with valid primary endpoint data were included in the primary analysis. For the primary outcome, the affected-side PD at 6–9 h was significantly greater in the RIC group than in the sham-RIC group (adjusted β = 12.166, 95% CI: 6.787–17.545; p < 0.001). Secondary analyses at other time points and of the unaffected side supported an acute physiological effect of RIC on dCA. These findings suggest that a single RIC session may rapidly improve impaired dCA in patients with ICAS and/or ECAS. Larger studies are needed to determine whether this response varies across clinical presentations and vascular territories.
